amendments.rule: Rule 53 decides a supplied verb by what is left in the clause to carry it, and that test does not turn on the verb being a copula. Where a verbless Greek clause has a prepositional predicate and the ASV supplies a **lexical** verb, the preposition carries it exactly as it carries a supplied *is* or *are*: `τὴν παρὰ τοῦ μόνου θεοῦ` → *that cometh from the only God* gives *cometh from* to `παρά`, as `τὰ παρ᾽ ὑμῶν` → *the things that came from you* gives *came from* to `παρ᾽`, and `ἵνα ἡμεῖς εἰς τὰ ἔθνη` → *that we should go unto the Gentiles* gives a bare *we* to the pronoun and *should go unto* to `εἰς`. An expressed subject does not change this, as `εἴ τις εἰς αἰχμαλωσίαν` → *If any man is for captivity* gives *any man* to `τις` and *is for* to `εἰς`; and rule 17 heads such a unit on the word realizing the preposition, not on the supplied verb. Rule 56 is the contrast and it is the narrow one: it gives the supplied verb to the subject only where the clause expresses no predicate at all, so that the subject is the sole token left to carry it. A prepositional phrase standing in the clause is such a predicate, and the recurring failure is reading the supplied verb off the English word order because the ASV writes it next to the subject. This rule reaches only a supplied verb that the standing prepositional phrase is the **predicate of**, and the test is which way the predication runs. Where the ASV instead supplies a **whole predicate of its own** — a lexical verb together with its own subject and complement — and the standing preposition is that supplied verb's **adjunct**, whose own English the ASV has already written in full, the supplied words answer to no token at all and are their own `added` unit under rule 5, the preposition keeping only the word written for it. `εἴτε διακονίαν, ἐν τῇ διακονίᾳ` → *or ministry, let us give ourselves to our ministry* marks *let us give ourselves* `added` and leaves `ἐν` a bare *to*, as `ὁ μεταδιδοὺς ἐν ἁπλότητι` → *he that giveth, let him do it with liberality* and `εἴτε προφητείαν κατὰ τὴν ἀναλογίαν τῆς πίστεως` → *whether prophecy, let us prophesy according to the proportion of our faith* do. An elliptical list is where this ordinarily arises, the Greek writing only the arguments of a predicate it never wrote; and the noun of such an item is ordinarily spent on its own English already, so rule 103's reasoning reaches the same answer from the other side. That the list is the ordinary case is not a scope: the operational test between the two arms is the supplied verb's **English subject**, and it is asked of any elliptical clause whatever its shape. Where that subject is some standing token's own English, a subject stands for the prepositional phrase to be predicated of and this rule's main arm folds the verb onto the preposition; where the ASV supplies the subject as well — a noun answering to no token of the verse, or a resumptive pronoun of a token whose English is already spent — nothing stands for the phrase to predicate of, and the supplied subject and verb are one `added` unit together. Every example above divides on that test: *that*, *the things that*, *we* and *any man* are the English of `τήν`, `τά`, `ἡμεῖς` and `τις`, while the *us* of *let us give ourselves* answers to nothing and the *him* of *let him do it* resumes an article already spent on *he*. So the test is availability and not bare expression, exactly as rule 76 reads rule 20's *present*. A **comparative correlative** whose clauses the Greek writes as bare prepositional strings is this same case and not a list, which is why `δι᾽ ἑνὸς παραπτώματος εἰς πάντας ἀνθρώπους εἰς κατάκριμα` → *through one trespass the judgment came unto all men to condemnation* marks the supplied *the judgment came* `added` whole and leaves each preposition the word written for it, while the neighbouring `τὸ μὲν γὰρ κρίμα ἐξ ἑνὸς εἰς κατάκριμα` → *the judgment came of one unto condemnation* folds its identical supplied *came* onto `ἐξ`, `κρῖμα` standing there to be predicated of. Do not split the supplied verb from the supplied subject, folding the one onto a preposition and adding the other: a standing prepositional phrase can be the predicate of a subject the Greek wrote and not of one the ASV wrote. A preposition whose English the ASV has written in full is not a word a supplied predicate can be a helper on, rule 27 forbidding a helper to be split from what licenses it and nothing here licensing this one. Rule 11 does not decide it either way: the ASV italicizes such a predicate only sometimes, and where it does the italics corroborate rather than license. Rules 63, 68, 75 and 96 are untouched, each of them naming a standing token that the supplied verb predicates of, and so is rule 53, whose supplied copula or auxiliary still folds onto an expressed predicate adjective, as `Ἡ ἀγάπη ἀνυπόκριτος` → *Let love be without hypocrisy* gives *Let ... be* to the adjective.
amendments.why: ROM.5.16 and ROM.5.18 put the identical supplied 'came', in the identical prepositional frame, on opposite arms of rule 62 within one chapter. The rule as written did not decide that pair: its stated test, 'which way the predication runs', is satisfied on both sides ('the judgment [is] unto all men to condemnation' predicates as readily as 'the judgment [is] of one'), and its only other guidance, 'an elliptical list is where this arises', reads as a scope limit that would exclude 5.18's comparative correlative altogether. The operational test added here — whether the supplied verb's English subject is some standing token's own English — divides every example the rule already carries, including the case that looks like a counterexample: 'he that giveth, let him do it with liberality' has a source token for the subject, yet the supplied predicate is `added`, because that token is already spent on 'he' and the supplied 'him' merely resumes it. That is rule 76's availability test, cited by number. The closing sentence forbids the halfway reading (fold the verb, add the subject), which is what a later pass would otherwise reach for on 5.18. The amendment changes no accepted edge: both ROM.5 verses already read as the amended rule requires.

conventions: The ASV's marginal alternative renderings and Greek glosses are not the target text, and nothing in this chapter was aligned to one. 5.1's 'Many ancient authorities read let us have', 5.2 and 5.3's 'Or, let us rejoice', and 5.20's 'Or, law' were set aside for the printed indicative and the printed 'the law'; 5.9 and 5.10's 'Greek in' gloss was set aside and ἐν takes the written 'by' at both places, as ἐν takes the written 'in' at 5.3, 5.5, 5.11, 5.13, 5.17 and 5.21. Rule 12 forbids remaking the source-side decision a margin bears on, and rule 97 makes a printed textual note corroboration only; neither licenses reading a margin as English to align.

In οὐ μόνον ... ἀλλὰ καί at 5.3 and 5.11, the ASV's supplied 'so' of 'not only so' rides inside μόνον's own unit as the completion of that adverb's English idiom, headed on 'only', with οὐ keeping 'not' and καί keeping 'also' as separate units. No corpus query on μόνος was made, and marking the 'so' `added` under rule 5 remains defensible, so a chapter meeting this idiom should query the lemma before following the reading rather than treating these two verses as settled precedent.

report: Checked every multi-treatment group in the candidate table plus the four `added` units, which the table is blind to. No cross-verse split found, so patches is empty.

οὕτως/καί: all five occurrences (5.12, 5.15, 5.18, 5.19, 5.21) read rule 100 — οὕτως takes the whole correlative headed on 'so', and καί is decided on its own by the English the ASV wrote ('also' at 5.15, 'and' at 5.12, nothing at 5.18/5.19/5.21). One analysis, not two.

Articles: the 75 occurrences divide cleanly by rules 19/20/21/23. The article takes a supplied 'our' only where no genitive pronoun competes (5.2, 5.3) and is empty where one does (5.5, 5.9, 5.10, 5.21) — rule 20's own stated contrast, written both ways in one chapter. 5.19's outer/inner pair (prenominal 'the one man's') against 5.15 and 5.17's postnominal 'the trespass of the one' is rule 57's two arms, decided by where the ASV puts the possessor.

Substantival adjectives: anarthrous δικαίου → 'a righteous man' headed on 'righteous' and ἀσεβῶν → 'the ungodly' headed on the adjective (5.7, 5.6), against articular τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ → 'the ... man' / 'good' headed on the supplied nominal (5.7). That is rules 17/58/102's own test — whether a Greek article stands to take the determiner — applied inside one verse, so no convention is needed.

Genitive absolutes: 5.6, 5.8 and 5.13 express their subject and give it the English subject word; 5.10 does not and the supplied pronoun rides with the participle. Rule 74's two arms, decided from the Greek and not from the English, which is nearly identical on both sides.

The one construction analysed two ways is the supplied 'came': folded onto the preposition at 5.16 (rule 62's main arm, κρίμα and χάρισμα expressed) and part of an `added` predicate at 5.18 (rule 62's added arm, the Greek writing bare prepositional strings with no subject). Source-licensed, already documented in 5.18's review note. I amended rule 62 to state the test operationally rather than patch either verse.

Supplied words that fold versus supplied words marked `added` were checked verse by verse, since the lemma table cannot see them: every folded word ('our', 'the', 'due', 'a', 'free', 'is', 'even', 'so' of 'not only so') has a token whose English it completes, and every `added` unit (5.9 'of God', 5.16 'so', 5.18's two predicates) has none. 5.16's `added` correlative 'so' and 5.3/5.11's folded 'so' are different words — one answers to a οὕτως the projection does not carry, the other completes μόνον's own idiom.

BSB: all eight disagreements are documented convention differences, not errors. 5.2 τῇ and 5.10/5.19 τοῦ/τῆς are rules 21/23 and 20/57 (no English determiner for the article to anchor); 5.5 τοῦ is rule 31's second attributive article, which says in terms that such a report is not a correction; 5.18/5.19/5.21 καί is rule 100, which says the same; 5.6 ἔτι is rule 97's mirror case, the projection carrying a doubled adverb the ASV writes once, cited to SBLGNT.ROM.5.6.v004 in the verse note. Nothing was changed to move the rate.

Thirteen notes repeated across verses; eleven of them restate rules 20, 21, 23, 32, 40, 65 and 100 and are left unrecorded. The two that are judgments rather than restatements are logged as conventions.
